episodes.167699: A cluster of storms produced large hail stones west of Granite Falls, near Olivia, and northeast toward the northwest suburbs of the Twin Cities. Most of these storms were elevated but had a steep lapse rate to generate large hail, up to 2 inches in diameter at times. ||These late morning, and early afternoon storms moved northeast out of Minnesota. A warm front lifted northward across southern Minnesota during the afternoon with a potent shortwave moving northeast out of Nebraska. This shortwave generated a large complex of storms and quickly moved northeast across southern Minnesota and produced numerous damaging wind gusts, tornadoes and hail. There were even some flooding concerns as three to five inches of rain fell across portions of west central and central Minnesota by the late evening as the storms diminished and moved off to the northeast.||Three tornadoes occurred within the large bow echo that surged from southwest Minnesota, northeast toward east central Minnesota. One occurred in Brown County, another in Sibley and Carver County, and a third in Anoka County. All of the tornadoes were rated EF0 and produced mainly tree and roof damage.||According to Xcel Energy, more than 75,000 customers were without power across southern Minnesota during the peak of the storm.
episodes.167700: A warm front lifted northward across southern Minnesota during the afternoon with a potent shortwave moving northeast out of Nebraska. This shortwave generated a large complex of storms and quickly moved northeast across southern and east central Minnesota before moving into west central Wisconsin by the evening. By the time it moved into west central Wisconsin, a large bow echo had formed and produced damaging wind gusts and hail.
episodes.167704: A cluster of severe thunderstorms that developed over South Dakota early Thursday morning, moved across west-central, and central Minnesota during the morning. Most of the hail fell across the central third of Minnesota, with some hail stones measured at 2 inches in diameter. In addition, a few mesonet wind sensors and the St. Cloud regional airport all reported severe wind gusts. There was also wind damage near Cold Spring and in central Morrison County where power outages occurred.
episodes.167705: A line of severe thunderstorms that developed across South Dakota and Nebraska during the afternoon of Thursday, May 12th, was a classic bow echo that surged north and east across western Minnesota. ||Temperatures in the mid to upper 90s along with dew points in the mid to upper 60s created ample instability for thunderstorms to develop ahead of a cold front, once the cap weakened during the evening. Despite fairly muggy dew points, the hot surface temperatures created inverted-V soundings that were primed for damaging wind potential. Thunderstorms came in three waves during the evening, as marginal shear values prohibited any long-lived or well-organized thunderstorms across the area.||Winds were measured by wind sensors at over 100 mph across portions of South Dakota, with a measured wind gust at Madison, Minnesota of 94 mph. There were also numerous measured wind gusts between 60 and 80 mph across west central and southwest Minnesota with embedded surges that produced a few tornadoes. The most concentrated area of damage based on reports of farm equipment, trailers, semis, trees, power lines, and other debris, occurred near the upper Minnesota River Valley, northward to Alexandria and Long Prairie.||Over Stevens County alone, structural damage was considerable as the majority of the damage was to farm outbuildings, sheds and grain bins. There were a few locations in the county where the main inhabited house or home structure did suffer loss of roof and siding and windows but those were more isolated in nature. Many locations had debris tossed a mile northeast from its parent location. Nearly 100% of the damage witnessed in Stevens county was consistent with a straight line wind event, with just one tornado crossing the southeast corner of the county.  ||Ten tornadoes were confirmed this day, with two in Lac Qui Parle County, including a house in Bellingham that had much of its roof removed.  In northwestern Swift County, a tornado tipped over trailers and various farm equipment was heavily damaged.  Two tornadoes were in Todd County, including one that moved through Clarissa.  Two more were in Morrison County, and one was on the east side of Lake Alexander, where many trees came down on vehicles, sheds, and cabins. A tornado also occurred in Douglas County, on the northwest side of Alexandria, where EF2 damage was noted.  The ninth tornado touched down south of Lowry in Pope County and was caught on video, and the tenth was in northwestern Stearns County, affecting the north side of Sauk Centre, and it was also caught on video.
episodes.167706: Storms that produced large hail across central and east central Minnesota during the morning and early afternoon hours of Thursday, May 12th, produced additional storms that afternoon over Rusk County. These storms produced large hail between Weyerhaeuser and Bruce.
episodes.167848: A severe thunderstorm developed over Tripp County, producing large hail over central and northeastern parts of the county.
episodes.167849: A thunderstorm became severe over the southern Black Hills and tracked northeast across the eastern Black Hills and adjacent plains. The storm produced large hail around quarter size and eventually strong wind gusts as it moved onto the plains.
episodes.167852: A severe thunderstorm developed over southern Meade County and tracked northeast through central and northeastern parts of the county. The storm produced large hail and damaging straight-line winds across the area, especially from Union Center to northeast of Red Owl. Southwest wind gusts of 70 to 80 mph caused some damage to property and outbuildings.
episodes.167855: Another severe thunderstorm developed and tracked across central and northeastern portions of Meade County, then through Ziebach County, producing large hail and gusty winds.
episodes.167856: A thunderstorm briefly became severe west of Spearfish, producing lots of small hail and a few stones around quarter size.
episodes.167907: Scattered thunderstorms again developed on the afternoon of the 11th as a weak upper level short wave approached the area. A deep upper level trough was able to keep a dryline backed up into eastern New Mexico this afternoon. Stronger deep layer shear was able to keep convection discrete on the 11th. One of the storms that developed generated hail up to two inches in diameter in far northern Castro County.
episodes.167988: Scattered thunderstorms developed along an instability ribbon from central to northeast Wisconsin during the afternoon hours on Thursday (5/12).  The strongest storms produced large hail across this area.  Further north, an outflow boundary caused wind damage across portions of north-central Wisconsin. Repeated rounds of moderate to heavy rain dumped upwards of 7 inches of rain across central Oconto County and southern Marinette County during the late afternoon and evening hours, causing $465,500 worth of damage to area roads and bridges across these counties.
episodes.167990: Thunderstorm tracked across central and north-central Wisconsin during the early morning hours on Thursday (5/12) north of a warm front and associated with a mesoscale convective vortex.  The strongest storm produced large hail up to quarter size as it tracked through central Wisconsin.
episodes.167991: Strong thunderstorms produced gusty winds as they tracked over the bay of Green Bay during the afternoon hours.
episodes.168263: Multiple days of light to moderate rain on top of saturated soils resulted in brief minor flooding for multiple rivers in the forecast area. Rainfall amounts for the 5 day period leading up to the flooding totaled just less than 3 inches near these river basins. Flooding developed on May 12th in the afternoon, with Mud Creek near Rauville peaking just at the flood stage of 9.0 feet before falling below flood stage on the morning of May 13th. Oak Creek near Wakpala reached a stage of 10.68 feet briefly before falling back below flood stage later that evening. The Big Sioux River near Castlewood also topped out at the flood stage of 9.0 feet and stayed at that level until the early morning hours of May 16th. No impacts were noted.
episodes.168267: Evening storms developed across western and south central South Dakota before expanding north and east through the course of the night, either as individual cells or as small clusters. Hail and wind damage was isolated but spread across the area. The bowing segment of a thunderstorm produced an estimated 70 mph wind gust west of Trail City, which knocked down a Cottonwood tree. One of the stronger clusters also generated hail up to the size of golf balls north of Oacoma, while another cluster moved into far eastern South Dakota and produce hail to half dollar size in Lake Poinsett later that morning.
episodes.168274: A derecho developed in south central South Dakota and traveled northeast into eastern and northeastern South Dakota. This thunderstorm complex generated 14 total tornadoes across northeastern South Dakota in addition to a broad area of straight-line wind damage with measured speeds up to 102 mph in Gary, SD. The damage swath was so large from this system that it encompassed most of northeastern South Dakota and western Minnesota, with damage to a countless number of homes and trees. The most impactful tornado was an EF-2 which damaged numerous homes in the town of Castlewood and drew national media attention. Governor Kristi Noem requested a Presidential Disaster Declaration, which was later granted, and signed Executive Order 2022-06 to help residents recover from related storm damage. Estimated statewide damage to public infrastructure is assessed at 6.7 million dollars across 20 counties and two reservations. South Dakota National Guard activated personnel to help with clear debris and provide security for the town of Castlewood during cleanup.
episodes.168275: A derecho developed in south central South Dakota and traveled northeast into western Minnesota. This thunderstorm complex generated 2 confirmed tornadoes across Big Stone and Traverse Counties, and produced a broad area of widespread and destructive straight-line winds in excess of 80 mph. Trees, buildings, power lines, grain bins, semi trucks, and other property was damaged or destroyed across west central Minnesota, and power outages lasted for multiple days in some cases.
episodes.168630: A fast moving cold front brought severe thunderstorms across portions of central into north central Nebraska during the afternoon hours of May 12. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 90 MPH and ping pong ball sized hail was reported. As the front lifted across the area later in the afternoon into the early evening hours, a dust storm developed. Visibilities were as low as a quarter mile and led to a multi vehicle accident along highway 30 in western Lincoln county. Strong wind gusts were also reported behind the exiting front with gusts up to 75 MPH reported.
episodes.168759: A broad upper level trough was over the Intermountain West. An upper level disturbance moved over West Texas. A dryline was across the area with fairly high moisture and instability to the east of this feature. Lift was enhanced from upslope flow across the Davis Mountains and Stockton Plateau. These conditions resulted in thunderstorms that produced hail in Pecos County.
episodes.168810: Thunderstorms occurred over central North Dakota during the early morning hours as a low level jet developed over the area. One storm became severe, producing estimated 60 mph wind gusts in Emmons County.
episodes.168846: Thunderstorms developed as a warm front lifted into central North Dakota and the James River Valley, where very strong deep layer shear and elevated instability were noted. A few storms became severe. The largest hail reported was ping pong ball size over McLean County.  The strongest wind gust reported was estimated at 80 mph, which caused tree and roof damage in Foster County.
episodes.169165: As a disturbance moved through the region, severe storms developed during the afternoon of May 12th. Given the warm, moist, and unstable environment present, storms were able to produce damaging winds.
episodes.169195: During the first week of the month, two storm systems moved out of the southern Plains. Scattered showers and thunderstorms brought around an inch of rain on average, while a few locations received up to 2.5 inches. Rises on the Ohio River were sufficient for some minor flooding in a few areas.
episodes.169205: There were two rounds of severe weather May 12 across Eastern Nebraska. The first occurred in the early morning in a region highlighted by a Moderate risk. This was mostly a wind risk with peak wind gusts measured or estimated near 75-80 mph.||The 2nd round of storms developed later in the evening and produced severe hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.169256: During the mid to late afternoon hours, scattered storms developed initially over Greeley and Wichita counties, then continued to form to the northeast across Northwest Kansas into Norton County. These storms produced hail up to quarters in size across portions of Greeley, Logan, and Thomas counties. As the storms began to decay, outflow produced high wind gusts up to 95 mph with damage in and near the town of Norcatur, KS in Decatur County.
episodes.169268: Morning and afternoon convection moved across parts of southern Minnesota along a warm front. Later in the afternoon, convection developed in South Dakota and moved into Northern Iowa and southern Minnesota as the upper level shortwave trough axis passed over. Remnant outflow boundaries from the morning convection helped to steer the convection, which strengthened into a well organized mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV). While the primary influences were over Minnesota, there was wind damage reported in northern Iowa with the trailing end of the convection.
episodes.169377: A line of storms moved across portions of southeast Minnesota during the morning of May 11th. These storms produced large hail that fell across parts of Dodge, Olmsted and Wabasha Counties. The largest reported hail was tennis ball sized southwest of Hammond (Wabasha County) and north of Plainview (Wabasha County). A second line of storms rolled across the region during the evening of the 11th. These storms also produced some hail with up to half dollar sized falling in Lake City (Wabasha County).
episodes.169401: During the late morning to midday hours, a line of storms developed along the dryline in Southwest Kansas, expanding north into Northwest Kansas. As the line moved across Norton and Graham counties, the storms produced up to half dollar sized hail and wind gusts up to 62 mph. Along with the storms, there was a wall of blowing dust that originated in extreme Southwest Nebraska and tracked southeast into portions of Northwest Kansas during the late afternoon. Visibility reductions as low as one-quarter mile were observed, with the greatest reductions in Decatur County.
episodes.169407: A few rogue storms produced severe sized hail across north central Kansas on May 12th, 2022.
episodes.169423: Major severe weather event unfolds across south central Nebraska during the afternoon and evening of May 12th, including wind gusts of 80 to 90 MPH. The most significant severe weather event of May 2022 occurred on a Thursday in which multiple rounds of thunderstorms wreaked havoc on essentially all of south central Nebraska at some point. The most intense severe weather, by far, was the first round. This activity actually developed over portions of west/southwest Kansas during the morning hours and moved northeast. Rapid intensification took place between 1PM and 2PM CDT as thunderstorms organized into a long line, and the first Severe Thunderstorm Warnings were issued for areas from Phillipsburg, KS to Lexington, NE. Initial storm reports ranged from quarter to ping pong ball size hail with the southern portion of the line, to widespread damaging wind gusts with the northern portion of the line across a large portion of Dawson County. Wind damage consisted of overturned pivots, uprooted trees, broken power poles, fence and roof damage, large tree limbs downed. Wind damage was widespread over central and western Dawson County where measured wind gusts of 60-70 MPH were common. Even an 82 MPH gust, which is considered ���significant severe���, was measured by a mesonet near Eddyville. Surface temperatures near 90 degrees and mixed layer CAPE values in excess of 3000 J/kg ahead of the line of thunderstorms, amidst 35kt to 50kt of southwesterly deep layer shear, allowed for continued intensification through the mid to late afternoon as the line raced northeast. Additional significant damaging wind impacts were felt across Sherman, Valley, and Greeley Counties. Valley County was another area especially hard hit. Here, several wind gusts in the 80-90 MPH range were reported, and damage was significant. Numerous trees were uprooted, pivots overturned, and outbuildings and grain bins destroyed. Another destructive aspect of this storm is that it also produced ping pong ball sized hail that was blown by the intense winds. This resulted in significant window and body damage to cars, as well as roof, siding, and window damage to homes. Additional significant wind damage was reported in and around Burwell (just barely outside this coverage area). The first round of thunderstorms exited north/northeast of the area around 3:30PM CDT, but the next round was ���hot on its heels���, and entered southern Nebraska around 4PM CDT, and quickly became severe. In fact, brief, but intense, circulations were noted on radar for a time just south and southeast of Hastings. This round affected mainly areas along and east of Highway 281. Since this region was spared from the first round, and a similar thermodynamic and kinematic environment was still in place, it���s no surprise that this round also intensified enough to produce ���significant severe��� wind gusts, most notably in a swath from Clay County northeast to Polk County. Several more 60-70 MPH wind gusts were reported in these areas, causing more overturned pivots, downed power lines, and damage to roofs, outbuildings, and grain bins. Also, intense wind gusts moved over Interstate 80 in Hamilton County, causing multiple overturned semis. This second round exited into eastern Nebraska and out of the Hastings CWA around 7PM CDT. The third and final round began to affect areas along and east Highway 183 between 7PM and 8PM CDT. The majority of this activity remained sub-severe as the greatest instability had been used up by the two previous rounds. However, a marginally severe wind gust of 59 MPH was measured at the Hastings airport shortly before 8PM. Thereafter, weakening ensued as the line became strung out and forward propagation slowed. Thunderstorms finally exited south central Nebraska between 11PM and midnight, ending a roughly 10 hour stretch of seemingly never ending severe weather!||Meteorologically speaking, this event was driven by a particularly volatile combination of intensifying shortwave ejecting from the central Rockies into the northern Plains, very unstable airmass (MUCAPE of 3000-4000 J/kg at it���s peak), and strong deep layer shear driven by 500 mb speed max of 60-70 kt. While this setup is not unheard of for mid-May, it���s certainly not very common, and for three distinct waves of thunderstorms to move through in a 10 hour period (two of which contained significant severe weather phenomena) is also not very common. From a regional perspective, the Hastings CWA was the developing grounds for a significant derecho that would propagate into the Northern Plains and Upper Mississippi Valley and go on to produce hundreds of measured severe wind gusts and wind damage reports, of which over 60 were considered ���significant severe���. Over 75 hail reports and nearly three dozen tornado reports were also reported, with the majority of tornadoes occurring in SD and MN. For 2022, this will likely be remembered as one of the most severe convective events of the year, both locally, and across the greater region.
episodes.169424: Significant severe weather event narrowly misses north central Kansas, bringing widespread thunderstorms, but only a single severe weather report on May 12th. A strong storm system brought multiple rounds of thunderstorms to the region on this day, with most of the severe weather occurring over south central Nebraska and points north. Please refer to the Storm Data entry for this event for Nebraska for more detailed information. The only severe weather report in north central Kansas came with the first round of thunderstorms during the early afternoon. Large hail up to ping pong ball size was reported in northwest Phillips County before this activity shifted north by around 2PM CDT. A second line of thunderstorms developed over Smith and Osborne Counties around 4PM. Severe thunderstorm warnings were issued for this activity, but no severe reports were received. This activity shifted northeast and east of the area shortly after 6PM. The third, and final, round of thunderstorms began to affect Rooks County around 7PM, and moved across the remainder of north central Kansas through the late evening hours. Similar to earlier in the day, some Severe Thunderstorm Warnings were issued, but no severe reports were received. Most of the strong activity ended by 10PM, though weak thunderstorms continued until around midnight.
episodes.169490: An upper disturbance moving through a warm, moist and unstable environment set the stage for the development of isolated severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall and flooding over portions of west and central Upper Michigan during the afternoon and evening of the 12th. Governor Whitmer declared a state of emergency for the flood damage in western Marquette County.
episodes.169492: A line of storms moved across portions of western Wisconsin during the morning of May 11th. A few of these produced hail and the largest reported was quarter sized near Alma (Buffalo County). A second round of storms in the evening also produced quarter size hail that fell in Nelson (Buffalo County).
episodes.169514: Strong to severe storms occurred across the far southeast plains on this day. Small hail was observed, however, winds gusted to 60 to 65 mph.
episodes.169627: Heavy rainfall from 2 to 3 inches from May 8 to May 12 across northeast into east central portions of South Dakota resulted in a brief period of minor flooding along the upper portions of the Big Sioux River.
episodes.169630: Heavy rainfall on May 11 from 1 to 3 inches in the Pipestone Creek and Redwood River Basins led to rapid runoff and a brief push into minor flood stage.
episodes.169723: A subtle upper level short wave trough moved across the southern Great Plains and combined with ample low level moisture ahead of a dryline, that was located on the New Mexico state line, to help produce scattered thunderstorms. Seventy six mph winds were recorded in Dalhart in association with some of the storms. Hail estimated at 2 inches in diameter was reported 3 miles east of Keyes, OK. Based on radar, the 81 mph wind gust 3 NNE of Umbarger was the result of virga. There were no thunderstorms and no lightning anywhre in the county at the time of occurrence. In addition, the dewpoint at this mesonet site plummeted from the middle 50's to the lower 30's during the wind gust.
episodes.169812: Isolated strong thunderstorms were observed over portions of south central Upper Michigan on the 12th.
episodes.169814: A strong thunderstorm was observed at Fairport during the early morning of the 12th.
episodes.169952: A warm front moving into the region during the afternoon hours of the 11th led to the development of severe thunderstorms across the area. As these storms moved across northwest Wisconsin during the evening hours, they produced small hail along with tree damage in the Spooner and Hayward areas before weakening and exiting the region.
episodes.169953: An area of thunderstorms moved across portions of east-central Minnesota during the afternoon hours of the 11th. One of the storms did produce minor tree damage in Pine County, but otherwise the storms were not severe. A wake low developed on the backside of the storms and let to strong winds that moved across the Aitkin area. These winds produced extensive damage at the Aitkin County fairgrounds along with knocking down numerous trees and removing roofs from sheds. Additionally, storms persisted through the night leading to isolated reports of flash flooding along the North Shore the following morning.
episodes.169954: A low pressure system moved northward from the Central Plains to the Northern Plains on May 12th and lifted a warm front across the Northland bringing two rounds of storms to the region. The first round during the afternoon hours were prolific hail producing storms with the largest hail stones being ping pong ball sized. Another round of storms arrived during the early evening hours and contained strong winds that moved through the Brainerd Lakes area. A maximum gust of 61 mph was recorded at the Brainerd Airport leading to widespread tree damage in the area. As storms continued overnight, heavy rainfall along the North Shore led to Flash Flooding in Lake and Cook counties with numerous road washouts reported.
episodes.169955: A low pressure system moved northward from the Central Plains to the Northern Plains on May 12th and lifted a warm front across the Northland bringing two rounds of storms to the region. The northwest Wisconsin area mainly saw impacts with the first round of storms with hail to 2 inches in diameter and numerous reports of trees down in the Spooner and Hayward areas.
episodes.169960: A low pressure system moved northward from the Central Plains to the Northern Plains on May 12th and lifted a warm front across the Northland bringing two rounds of storms to the region. With Lake Superior still being cold, this stable air at the surface prevented much of the winds in the storms to reach the surface. However, a few gusts were reported at Silver Bay and Port Wing with the strongest gust being 48 mph at Silver Bay during a storm during the late evening.
episodes.170188: A severe thunderstorm developed across Mobile County and produced large hail.
episodes.170209: A pre-frontal trough brought thunderstorms into the area during the evening of May 11. Isolated severe thunderstorms brought hail up to 1.5 inches and wind gusts of 58 mph, along with localized street flooding.
episodes.170212: A strong cold front and upper low traversed the area during the afternoon and evening of May 12th. During the afternoon, a larger scale Derecho moved from northeastern Nebraska, through eastern South Dakota and into portions of far southeastern North Dakota and west-central Minnesota. Widespread strong to severe thunderstorms were observed, with large hail, tornadoes, and damaging wind gusts all being reported during this time.
episodes.170323: Several thunderstorms out of the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles collapsed with gust fronts extending into mainly southern counties across the CWA. A heat burst over these counties was the main cause of the high winds with a warning in place as up to 70 mph winds were reported. DCAPE values of over 1000 J/kg over the area with an already instilled gradient that allowed for such strong gusts. Another round of severe storms pushed out of the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles late evening into Morton County and moved northeast through sunset weakening with time. Shear profiles were weak, less than 30kts, within this marginal risk of western Kansas. Damaging winds and hail were the main threat with just a handful of reports near and around Elkhart.
episodes.170324: Thunderstorms formed ahead of a dryline along and east of Hwy 283 in an area of slight risk becoming linear and more of a damaging wind event. Small hail and winds up to 60mph were reported. Shear profiles were relatively weak less than 30 kts and with dewpoints in the 60s, ample CAPE values up to 1500 J/kg were evident.
episodes.170470: A gusty shower moved over the Chesapeake Bay on the night of May 11.
episodes.170478: A volatile environment featured a warm front from parts of east central South Dakota into western Minnesota, with a dryline extending to the southwest into Nebraska. With a very strong wave moving northeast through Nebraska into a highly unstable and highly sheared environment, scattered storms initiated and quickly grew upscale to a broad linear structure with damaging winds. With crop development well behind schedule and many fields yet to be planted, there was ample dirt available to be lofted into the leading edge of the storms, which took on the characteristics of a haboob reducing visibility to near zero at the onset of high winds.||A broad swath of winds from 70 to 100 mph devastated much of southeast South Dakota, and portions of southwest Minnesota, northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, causing extensive tree and structural damage and scores of injuries. The highest observed wind gust was 107 mph near Tripp, SD. In addition, vehicles and high profile vehicles were blown off several roads, shutting down traffic on Interstates 29 and 90. Two (direct) fatalities occurred in vehicles impacted by debris as the storms moved into the Sioux Falls area. Power was disrupted in a widespread area, with estimates of over 45,000 customers impacted at one time. Many schools were closed due to damage and power issues. The South Dakota Governor requested and was granted a Presidential Disaster Declaration for damage to public infrastructure at an estimated cost of 6.7 million dollars across 20 counties and two reservations. Private losses were a much higher toll, and just one of the impacted counties (McCook) estimated at least 150 to 175 million dollars in damage. Presidential Disaster Declarations were also granted in Dixon County, Nebraska and Lincoln County, Minnesota. ||Following the afternoon line of storms, a secondary band of storms developed near the core of the upper level jet across eastern Nebraska in the early evening hours. These storms also quickly become severe, with a mix of large hail, damaging wind, and even an isolated tornado near Sioux City. This cluster of storms moved through far southeast South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening.
episodes.170479: Elevated instability and a strengthening low-level jet developed a complex of thunderstorms which built southward into the Highway 14 corridor overnight. Isolated large hail fell with the strongest storm near De Smet.
